summary:
Visitors to Pennsylvania stand under the United States federal framework. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth, the State Department has stopped processing the X marker and will issue passports only as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, and passports already carrying X remain valid until expiry. The ACLU is suing the State Department over the changed treatment of trans passports, and the Supreme Court has allowed the Department to proceed. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 separately bar visas for trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events, with applicants flagged under the internal code SWS25, and a declared gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud carrying a permanent bar.

Checkpoint screening carries a separate risk of involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

A national anti-trans legal-risk assessment in its July 2026 update places Pennsylvania in its low-risk tier, covering states that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specially protecting them, while recording that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights nationally alongside the federal measures driving that trend.

The legislative pressure in Pennsylvania is concentrated on youth school sports rather than on transgender adults or on facility access. The state Senate passed Senate Bill 1293, the Save Women's Sports Act, on 22 April 2026; the measure would bar transgender female athletes from girls' and women's teams in the commonwealth. Governor Josh Shapiro called supportive lawmakers extremists, and it was unclear whether the House of Representatives would take the bill up. The Senate had already approved an earlier version, Senate Bill 9, on 6 May 2025, reserving teams designated for women to biological females in K-12 and collegiate sport and sending it to the House, with sponsors including Senators Judy Ward and Kristin Phillips-Hill.

Governor Tom Wolf vetoed comparable legislation on 11 July 2022. That bill would have required public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed, with athletes in female-designated sports required to have been assigned female at birth; it had passed the Republican-led legislature largely on party-line votes.

A national equality tracker records no public-facility-use ban for Pennsylvania, so the restroom exposure a visitor faces in the state is set by federal and airport rules rather than by any state restriction on facility use.
tangentialFactors:
Facility restrictions are a live risk outside Pennsylvania. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, additional states impose outright bans on facility use by gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student who announced he was there to break the law used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol and was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Identity documents vary sharply by state. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, which rights groups describe as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and on what conditions.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated.

Foreign governments have responded to the federal document and data rules with public warnings. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues. Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.
localsOnly:
The restrictions advancing in the Pennsylvania legislature affect residents' children rather than adult residents directly. Senate Bill 1293 passed the Senate on 22 April 2026 and would reserve girls' and women's teams in the commonwealth to athletes assigned female at birth, and Senate Bill 9 cleared the same chamber on 6 May 2025 with the same effect for K-12 and collegiate sport. Governor Josh Shapiro's public opposition and Governor Tom Wolf's 11 July 2022 veto of the earlier bill indicate that enactment has so far turned on the governor's office as much as on the chamber majorities.

The July 2026 risk assessment places Pennsylvania among states that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specially providing for them, which describes an absence of hostile legislation rather than a protective statutory scheme.

Residents navigating gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates must work from the state-by-state conditions set out in the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map; the sources in hand do not state Pennsylvania's own conditions for those changes.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in the sources: whether the Pennsylvania House of Representatives will take up Senate Bill 1293 or Senate Bill 9, and whether either becomes law. The record reflects Senate passage and gubernatorial positions only.

Not sourced in this inventory: Pennsylvania's own rules for changing gender markers on driver's licences and birth certificates; any state hate-crime enhancement covering anti-trans offences; state limits on gender-affirming care; recognition of marriages and partners; and any state-level protection machinery specific to trans residents.

The finding that Pennsylvania has no public-facility-use ban reflects a national equality tracker's current record and does not resolve how individual school districts, municipalities or private venues set restroom policy, nor whether enforcement of any facility rule has been attempted in the state.

The low-risk tier in the July 2026 assessment is a comparative grading against other states, not a finding that no anti-trans measure has been introduced in Pennsylvania; two such bills reached Senate passage.
